title: An education plan for Democratic governors
author: Josh Cowen
source: The Forum with Josh Cowen (joshcowen.substack.com), September 25, 2026
summary: In the second part of his education agenda, Josh Cowen turns to what Democratic governors should prioritize after November, arguing that states remain the primary drivers of education policy and may matter even more if federal spending pulls back. He organizes his advice by political context. With a Democratic trifecta, governors should use their power for genuinely weighted school funding, focused goals in literacy, math, attendance, and tutoring, investment in educators, statewide measurement, universal pre-K, and career and technical education, all as one education journey from birth to adulthood. Under divided government or a Republican legislature, the priorities narrow toward protecting funding, showcasing successful public schools, and building coalitions for future openings. He closes with three steps every Democratic governor can take: demand a federal education stress test, pick five outcomes rather than fifty-five priorities, and make the state the place where public education gets better.
points: Cowen argues states have historically been the main policy drivers in education and may need to fill federal gaps.
He cites Michigan's move toward a true weighted foundation allowance for disadvantaged students and English learners.
Governors should choose three or four measurable district goals and align money, training, data, and accountability to them.
Universal pre-K and early education may become crucial if Head Start is dismantled or restructured.
Every Democratic governor should conduct a federal education stress test and build a state financial resilience plan.
quotes: With a possible federal spending pullback, and the fact that states have historically been the primary policy driver when it comes to education, this question is probably even more important than a federal plan.
Simply put: Use the power. This is where progressives can be the most ambitious relative to other states and to a federal education agenda.
Governors should pick three or four things they want every school district in the state to get better at—and then align money, training, data and accountability around them.
Early education may become extremely important on the state level if Trump succeeds in demolishing Head Start, or at least severely altering its administrative structure.

A Democratic trifecta should be able to build a coherent state strategy around early childhood, K-12, CTE and college, and into the workforce rather than treating these as separate agencies and constituencies.
Even if the federal government becomes smaller, more hostile, or simply less reliable, states aren’t powerless. In fact, they remain the key actors in American education.
Democrats should be the party that makes the public education system feel useful across a person’s entire life.
